prompt.context: Portkey Inc. is a British company that has developed a new technology, Apparate, that can transport a person in a matter of seconds. The founder, Albus Severus Potter, invented the technology when he needed a fast way to travel from McMuggle to the Hogwarts School of Management. Apparate is the first technology of its kind, patented and does not have any direct competitors. Up-front fixed costs are estimated to be 2.3BN GBP.
prompt.question: Albus has tasked us with figuring out whether to launch Apparate, and if launched – how to price this new service.

clarifying_info.q: In which markets can Apparate operate?
clarifying_info.a: The U.K. is the only country that has given regulatory approval.

clarifying_info.q: Is there any consumer interest data?
clarifying_info.a: From an initial consumer survey, 60% of travelers indicated they are open to this new mode of travel.
From initial testing, out of 200,000 people, one person experienced half-a-body delay – an often fatal condition. The technology's risks also increase as trip distance increases.
To determine whether to launch Apparate and, if so, at what price.

exhibits.title: UK Travel Market Statistics
exhibits.shows: A table of statistics about the UK travel market for a 400-mile trip (e.g., London to Edinburgh), including population figures, traveler percentages, ticket prices, trip frequency by segment, and growth rate.

framework: Enter market? – assess whether Portkey Inc. should launch Apparate at all
Market attractiveness – market size, growth trends, consumer interest, competitive landscape, regulatory environment
Pricing – value-based vs. cost-based pricing; comparison to substitutes; willingness to pay
Other considerations – safety/risks, further product development, pilot strategy

questions.prompt: Calculate the potential size of the market for a 400-mile trip (e.g., London to Edinburgh), focusing on the UK market for 400-mile airplane trips.
questions.guidance: Candidate should break the market into Price × Quantity and recognize two customer segments: business and leisure travelers. After brainstorming the inputs needed (population, % that travel, segment split, trip frequency, ticket price), the interviewer provides Exhibit A. Candidate should note the market is large and growing at 2% per year. A strong candidate may also note that business tickets tend to be pricier and could compute a breakeven check.

math.setup: Total Market = Business segment revenue + Leisure segment revenue. Revenue = (UK population) × (% that travel) × (% in segment) × (trips/year) × (price/trip).
steps: Breakeven check (bonus): 2.3BN fixed costs ÷ 100 GBP per trip = 23MM trips needed = ~8% market share of trip volume
math.answer: 30.4BN GBP total addressable market; ~304MM trips annually.

questions.prompt: As a next step, assess pricing strategies. What price would you recommend?
questions.guidance: Candidate should construct a brief second framework covering value-based pricing versus cost-based pricing. Key points: Apparate should be value-based priced because there is no direct competition, the breakeven is achievable at current substitute prices, and substitutes (plane tickets) are already ~100 GBP. Candidate may also mention target return pricing (set price to achieve breakeven in 1 year) or psychological pricing (high price as quality signal). Candidate should NOT be anchored to the 100 GBP figure in Exhibit A as the ceiling — it is the floor (at minimum match substitute price). Strong candidates will brainstorm how to value time saved (work hours, opportunity cost) to justify a premium. Candidate may also note that hesitant early adopters may require a promotional discount.

recommendation: Portkey Inc. should move forward with launching Apparate.
The market for short-haul UK trips is 30.4BN GBP and growing at 2% per year.
There are no direct competitors and the technology is patented, providing strong pricing power.
A value-based pricing strategy would position the company for future growth while funding further R&D.
risks: Safety risk: product malfunction (1 in 200,000 users experienced a potentially fatal half-a-body delay).
Consumer adoption risk: travelers may be hesitant to adopt a radically new mode of transport.
Regulatory risk: currently approved only in the UK; restrictions could limit geographic expansion.
Competitive entry risk: future competitors could undercut value-based pricing.
next_steps: Complete a rigorous, publicly available safety study to build consumer confidence.
Conduct market research to better understand consumer needs and willingness to pay.
Select a pilot market and/or segment (e.g., business travelers) and run a controlled test launch.
